newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Sweden should join EMU from 1999 - central bank.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sweden should join EMU from 1999 - central bank.

text.p: Sweden's powerful central bank ended months of fence-sitting on Friday to come down firmly on the side of Swedish membership of European economic and monetary union (EMU), saying it should be among first wave to join in January 1999.
The Riksbank said in a statement that it rejected the conclusions of an official inquiry into Swedish EMU membership, saying the report had underestimated the benefits to the country.
"Our possibility to have an impact on the development of the union would be less if we stayed outside," Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom told Reuters Financial Television.

"The economic benefits and the possibility of influencing the future direction of monetary policy lead the Riksbank's governing board to conclude that Sweden should participate ...from the start," the bank said in a separate statement.
The central bank, with Friday's announcement, has become the first major public institution in Sweden to throw its weight behind membership of the future single currency.

The government has called for a wide public debate on membership but the cabinet -- originally pro-EMU -- has cooled considerably because of opinion polls showing strong public distate for monetary union.
No Swedish minister, including Prime Minister Goran Persson, has expressed support for Swedish EMU membership since opinion polls showed strong disquiet.

An official report by Professor Lars Calmfors published last month concluded that the risks of EMU membership were severe and that Sweden should not be in the first European Union (EU) nations to join.
The Riksbank said that the Calmfors report was over-cautious and underestimated the benefits of joining.
Backstrom said Sweden's influence on monetary union would be greater if the country joined EMU from its earliest start date of January 1, 1999.

"Many Swedes have a reluctant view on this membership issue but I've also said that, looking at our history, we have always participated in similar arrangements, the gold standard, Bretton Woods and we have had very good experience from doing that," he said.

"I believe that if this issue was discussed more in coming months I think the Swedish population could have the possiblity to make up their minds and not only be reluctant as the case has been so far," he said.

The Swedish crown is currently under growing pressure from suspicions that the government is caving in on its earlier pledges to be fiscally tough and that Sweden may stay outside the EU's currency union.
The uncertainty has led to increased volatility in the currency that has weakened significantly in recent weeks.
The currency is now as weak against the dollar as it was a year ago. On February 13 last year the crown was trading at 7.4166 to the dollar and on February 7 this year it was trading at 7.4291.
Against the mark the crown has shown similar weakness since the start of September 1996 when the currency was trading at 4.4860 crowns to the mark.
